newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK red chips steal spotlight from blue chips.
newsitem.headline: HK red chips steal spotlight from blue chips.

text.p: Hong Kong investors have turned the spotlight on red chip companies, prodding them into asset expansion by bidding up their shares and encouraging them to raise funds for acquisitions, analysts said on Wednesday.
China Pharmaceutical Enterprise & Investment Corp Ltd is the latest of the red chips -- mainland Chinese firms incorporated in Hong Kong -- to tap the market for funds.
It said on Wednesday it would issue 168 million new shares at HK$1.2768 per share to finance acquisitions.
The share price had surged 15 percent this month before the announcement on expectations that red chips would benefit from asset injections from their China parents.

"The market is making them do it. Basically, what the public is doing is raising the price and saying: 'Here, I'll pay a bit more money for your stock, now will you inject?'" said Charles de Trenck, China strategist at UBS Securities.
"You need to have a substantial market cap to do a placement to acquire something. That is the concept driving the higher price," he said.
Last month, Guangzhou Investment Co Ltd raised HK$1.24 billion to finance acquisitions. Its shares rose 19 percent in the two weeks preceding the announcement.

"Investors think that once the company gets the placement done, they have got cash to do asset acquisitions and that is the key momentum for growth," said Jason Cheung, China analyst at Morgan Stanley.
Once the placement is done, the structure of the company changes, said de Trenck. "The equity base grows, the gearing drops and the company becomes a totally different animal."
Investors justify the premiums at which red-chip companies trade compared with the blue chips by the potential they have for acquiring assets at attractive prices from parent companies.

"The red chips are evaluated not so much on their existing portfolios as on their prospects of acquiring good-quality assets at generous prices in the future," said Nikko Research Center in a recent report.

It said most red-chip parent companies were under the direct supervision of China's State Council, wholly owned by municipal governments, or managed by China's "princelings" -- the progeny of Chinese leaders.
"Red chips are, therefore, viewed as 'guanxi' (connection) plays," Nikko Research Center said.

With Hong Kong's handover to China at midnight on June 30, investors are betting that further economic integration will propel the red chips -- generally diversified entities -- into major conglomerates.
"They are really China showpieces," said Pauline Gately, regional strategist at Merrill Lynch.
"The interest is to shape these companies and promote them as heavyweights in the Hang Seng Index after 1997," she said.
Market favourites include China Overseas Land and Investment Ltd, China Resources Enterprise Ltd, COSCO Pacific Ltd, Ng Fung Hong Ltd and Shanghai Industrial Holdings Co Ltd.

However, with the blue-chip sector currently under consolidation, the fever for China plays has spread into some smaller red-chip companies which might not have the same potential for asset expansion, analysts said.
"This is the ideal time for everyone to float their silly idea," said Marshall Mays, chief strategist at Nikko Research Center.
"That is what happens in a bull market. You can get your financing in that kind of exuberant market."
